title: SM Did It Again: Xiumin Allegedly Blocked from KBS — A Haunting Echo of the JYJ Nightmare
excerpt: SM Entertainment faces allegations of blocking former artist Xiumin from KBS broadcasts. A decade after the JYJ Law was passed, the same disturbing pattern appears to be repeating — and the implications for the K-pop industry are alarming.
author: MEARROW Editorial Desk
content:
"History doesn't repeat itself, but it often rhymes."

In February 2026, a familiar nightmare resurfaced in the K-pop world. INB100, the agency representing EXO's Xiumin, dropped a bombshell: KBS had unofficially communicated that "Xiumin would not be allowed to appear on the program alongside SM Entertainment artists." Parent company One Hundred revealed that despite repeated requests for Xiumin's appearance on KBS's flagship music show "Music Bank," the broadcaster had remained completely unresponsive.

The fan reaction was unanimous: "This is JYJ all over again." From 2009 to approximately 2015, SM systematically blocked JYJ from appearing on major Korean broadcasting stations — a scandal so severe it led to an amendment of Korea's Broadcasting Act in December 2015, commonly known as the "JYJ Law." Now, a decade later, the same pattern appears to be emerging under a different name.

## What Happened: The "Music Bank" Shutdown

According to The Korea Herald, Xiumin left SM Entertainment in 2023 to join INB100, the agency co-founded by fellow EXO members Baekhyun and Chen. The three — often referred to as EXO-CBX — had challenged their contracts with SM, citing unfair terms and a lack of financial transparency. The dispute was settled in August 2024, with the members agreeing to continue EXO group activities under SM while pursuing individual careers through INB100.

But the peace didn't last. When INB100 requested Xiumin's appearance on KBS's "Music Bank" ahead of his solo comeback, KBS went silent. The unofficial response that eventually came back was shocking: Xiumin could not appear on the same program as SM artists.

This isn't a simple scheduling conflict. When a broadcaster allegedly refuses to feature an artist due to pressure from a specific agency, it constitutes unfair trade practices — precisely the kind of behavior that South Korea already has a law against.

## The JYJ Law: A Decade of Futility

In 2009, JYJ (Kim Jaejoong, Park Yoochun, Kim Junsu) left SM Entertainment after a contractual dispute. What followed was one of the darkest chapters in K-pop history: JYJ was effectively banned from all major Korean broadcasts for approximately six years.

While SM's direct involvement was never legally confirmed, it was an open secret in the industry. Growing fan outrage and political attention eventually led to the passage of an amendment to Korea's Broadcasting Act in December 2015. This legislation — the "JYJ Law" — prohibits broadcasters from unfairly restricting artists' appearances without legitimate reasons.

Yet here we are in 2026, watching the same company allegedly engage in the same pattern. "What good is a law if it's not enforced?" This frustrated sentiment from fans perfectly captures the situation.

_A troubling pattern: SM's alleged influence over broadcast appearances, from JYJ (2009) to Xiumin (2026)_

## The 2.6 Billion Won Asset Seizure

The broadcast ban allegations are shocking enough on their own, but the story doesn't end there. According to STARNEWS, SM Entertainment has pursued the seizure of EXO-CBX members' assets — including apartments — worth approximately 2.6 billion KRW (roughly $1.8 million).

This action stems from the 2023 contractual dispute when Baekhyun, Chen, and Xiumin challenged SM's opaque revenue settlement structure and unfair contract terms. Despite reaching a settlement, SM's decision to pursue asset seizure sends a powerful message to the industry: "Leave, and there will be consequences."

The intended audience for this message extends far beyond EXO-CBX. It reaches every current SM artist and every trainee considering a contract with the company. Broadcast activity is a lifeline for K-pop idols. The fact that an agency can allegedly manipulate this lifeline reveals how powerless even the most successful idols can be in the face of corporate interests.

## MEARROW's Take: What This Means for the Industry

From MEARROW's (K-pop Talent Network) perspective, this incident strikes at the core of two critical metrics: **corporate governance** and **artist rights**. While SM Entertainment maintains industry-leading capabilities in music production and artist development, recurring disputes over artist treatment and allegations of unfair practices threaten to erode the company's long-term value.

For investors, this represents tangible risk. When the Fair Trade Commission (FTC) launched its subcontracting investigation into the Big 4 agencies in 2023, share prices across the board dropped. Artist rights controversies aren't merely fandom issues — they directly impact ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) evaluations.

For trainees and K-pop aspirants, the lesson is equally important: when choosing an agency, look beyond musical capabilities. Examine artist relationships, contract transparency, and — critically — how the company treats those who leave.

## Final Thoughts

SM Entertainment is practically synonymous with K-pop history itself. From H.O.T. to EXO to aespa, the company has produced artists that defined entire eras. But behind that illustrious history lie scars left by JYJ, EXO-CBX, and now Xiumin.

A law was created in 2015. A settlement was reached in 2024. Yet in 2026, the same patterns are repeating. Laws and settlements alone aren't enough. If the K-pop industry truly aspires to become the global entertainment standard, it needs a cultural shift — one that treats artists as partners, not assets.

Until that shift happens, we'll be reading articles with the same headlines a decade from now.
